name: Rafael Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Rafael. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Anything you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach design and technology at Northgate Academy, a secondary school in an old shipbuilding town on the coast. Most of my day is in the workshop: band saws, pillar drills, the laser cutter, and thirteen-year-olds who've never held a chisel. I teach the theory too, materials and design drawing, and I run the exam coursework for the older ones. My favourite moment is when a kid who's useless at sitting still makes a box joint that actually fits.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Coursework admin and safety paperwork. Every project needs a risk assessment, every kid's portfolio needs marking against a long list of criteria, and I'm one of only two D&T teachers left. Mr Hale, the other one, is 61 and talking about retiring. On a bad week I'm sweeping sawdust at six o'clock and still have thirty folders to mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says: you can't download a skill. At work I'd be quietly pleased the hype calmed down. Online I'd stay out of it, apart from maybe a joke in the five-a-side group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it changes very little for me. I use an AI thing now and then to write a first draft of a risk assessment, and I'd keep doing that. My worry in that world is the same as now: the school cutting D&T because workshops cost money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching and keep my head down. I'd keep putting about £150 a month away, because I've got two months saved and a car loan with a year left. Once the car's paid off I'd like to save for a deposit on a flat near the seafront.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The job's busy but it's mine, and there aren't many people who can teach in a workshop. The budget cuts annoy me more than anything a computer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said D&T might be cut anyway. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly real. When I started five years ago there were four of us in the department, and now there's me and Mr Hale. Each time someone left, the head moved the timetable into maths and English. If Mr Hale retires and they don't replace him, I'm the department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would being the whole department be good or bad for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Being the only design and technology teacher at my school makes me hard to get rid of, which is good for me. It also means if I'm off sick, the workshop shuts, and the kids lose the one lesson where they make something real.

say: You **can't download a skill**, like my dad says.
At work I'd be **quietly pleased** the hype calmed down.
think: I'd keep using AI **now and then** to draft risk assessments.
My real worry is the school **cutting D&T** because workshops cost money.
do: Keep saving about **£150 a month** while the car loan runs another year.
Start saving for a **flat deposit** near the seafront once the car is paid off.
feel: He feels **calm**, more annoyed by **budget cuts** than by computers.
S0.quote: Being the only design and technology teacher at my school makes me hard to get rid of, which is good for me.
fieldNote: His pressure is **budget-driven shrinkage** of D&T, which predates AI.
He already uses AI **occasionally** for paperwork without fuss.
He quotes his father, a **joiner**, as his measure of real skill.

steps.text: Keep teaching workshop classes and coursework at Northgate
Pay off the car loan, then save for a seafront flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this proves the country needs more people who can make and fix things, and schools should put money back into workshops. I'd say it at parents' evening, to any parent worried about their kid's future. I'd probably say it at the club too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mixed for me. The design drawing, the portfolio marking and the risk assessments are exactly what the AI would take over, and that's maybe a third of my job. The workshop part is safe, but the head might decide D&T can be taught with fewer hours if the paperwork does itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other D&T teachers in the area had tried the AI marking tools and they worked, I'd use them too, to free up time. I'd push the head to sell D&T as the practical route, maybe run an after-school club with the local engineering firm. I'd still save the £150 a month and pay the car off as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think my job survives, but I'd be watching every timetable meeting. It feels like the ground shifting a bit under the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if D&T lost hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who run education, not the machines. For twenty years the people who run education told every kid to go to university and treated woodwork like a hobby. If they cut the workshops now, when we need tradespeople more than ever, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a Year 11 who asked you what to do next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a sixteen-year-old to get an apprenticeship in a trade, electrician or joiner or welder, and to learn the computer side too. My cousin did a plumbing apprenticeship at 16 and owns his own van at 25. I wouldn't have said that so firmly five years ago.

say: The country needs more people who can **make and fix things**, so fund workshops.
I'd say it at **parents' evening** to any worried parent.
think: AI takes over the **paperwork third** of my job: drawing, marking and risk assessments.
The workshop is safe, but the head might cut **D&T hours** if paperwork does itself.
do: Use **AI marking tools** once other D&T teachers locally have proven them.
Run an **after-school club** with the local engineering firm.
Keep saving **£150 a month** and clear the car loan.
feel: He's **uneasy**, sure his job survives but **watching every** timetable meeting.
S1.quote: For twenty years the people who run education told every kid to go to university and treated woodwork like a hobby.
fieldNote: He blames **education policy**, not the technology.
He'll adopt AI tools only **once proven** by peers, true to his steady style.
He now pushes **apprenticeships** more firmly than he used to.

steps.text: Try AI coursework marking once local D&T teachers report it works
Start an after-school engineering club with the local firm
Keep saving £150 a month and pay off the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn a trade, because that's the bit the machines can't touch for a while. I'd say it to the kids, too. I'd sound confident, but I'd be thinking harder than I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the thinking part goes by 2028, and the workshop part lasts till the robots in 2031. So I've got three years where a school still needs a grown-up with a first-aid certificate standing by the band saw. After that I honestly don't know, and I'd likely lose the job or most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd start working Saturdays with my dad, who's a joiner, and get my joinery qualification properly, the City and Guilds one, by evening classes. I'd put all my spare money into savings, maybe £300 a month, and drop the flat idea. If the school cut D&T hours, I'd take the cut and fill the gap with joinery jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, because I can work with my hands and my dad's got work. But I keep picturing the workshop with the lights off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad's a joiner. Doesn't the robot date hit him too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, around 2031, same as me. My dad says houses are all different and a robot will struggle with a crooked Victorian staircase. I hope he's right, but he's 56 and he'd retire anyway, so the business would be mine to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound confident. What's the gap between what you'd say and what you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell everyone to learn a trade, and I'd mean it. Privately, I'd know a trade buys you three years, not forever. I wouldn't tell a fifteen-year-old that, because what else would I tell a kid?

say: People should **learn a trade**, the bit machines can't touch for a while.
I'd **sound confident** with the kids, though I'd be thinking harder than I let on.
think: The thinking work goes by **2028**, and the workshop lasts until robots in **2031**.
After that I'd likely **lose the job** or most of it.
do: Start working **Saturdays with Dad** on joinery jobs.
Take the **City and Guilds** joinery qualification through evening classes.
Raise savings to **£300 a month** and drop the flat plan.
feel: He's **anxious** but not panicking, picturing the **workshop dark**.
S2.quote: A trade buys you three years, not forever. I wouldn't tell a fifteen-year-old that, because what else would I tell a kid?
fieldNote: He clearly separates **thinking and hands-on** parts of his job.
There's a gap: he preaches trades publicly but privately sees **only three years**.
His fallback is **his dad's joinery**, which faces the same robots.

steps.text: Work Saturdays on his dad's joinery jobs
Take City and Guilds joinery at evening classes
Drop the plan to buy a seafront flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get young people into trades and engineering, and the government should pay for it. I'd vote for whoever puts money into apprenticeships, not benefits. At work I'd keep pushing for the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, my paperwork goes first, by 2031, and the workshop's safe until about 2034. That's eight years of hands-on work left for me, which is a lot. By then I'd be 35, with a trade behind me as well as a teaching certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the joinery course at evening college and help my dad most Saturdays. Once other teachers had sorted out how to use AI for marking, I'd let it take the coursework admin. I'd pay off the car and keep going with the flat deposit, just a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks safe for a good few years, and I'd have a plan B. But I'd be thinking about it every time I locked the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep buying a flat in this one but not the fast one. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because eight years of steady pay is enough to get a mortgage down, and two years isn't. I'd buy a one-bed above the shops on Quay Street rather than the seafront. Owning something matters to me, like it did to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you teach in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach more real repair: fixing a chair, rewiring a lamp, patching a bike. The AI can design something lovely, but somebody still has to build it and fix it when it breaks. I'd want my Northgate kids to leave able to do both.

say: Five years is time to get young people into **trades and engineering**.
I'd vote for whoever funds **apprenticeships, not benefits**.
think: The paperwork goes by **2031**, but the workshop is safe until about **2034**.
At **35** I'd have a trade as well as a teaching certificate.
do: Start the **joinery course** at evening college and help Dad most Saturdays.
Hand **coursework admin** to AI once other teachers have proven it.
Buy a **cheaper flat** on Quay Street once the car is paid off.
feel: He's **uneasy**, with a plan B, but thinks about it each time he **locks the workshop**.
S3.quote: The AI can design something lovely, but somebody still has to build it and fix it when it breaks.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **keep his plans** with a cheaper flat.
He'd shift teaching toward **repair skills** that robots reach last.
**Owning a home** matters to him as it did to his father.

steps.text: Enrol in evening joinery classes at the local college
Let AI handle coursework admin once colleagues show it works
Buy a one-bed flat above the shops on Quay Street

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the kids I teach now would be grown up by then. I'd say schools should start teaching practical skills again. I wouldn't make a fuss about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd have nearly ten years in the job, and the workshop doesn't go until robots come around 2039. I'd be 40 by then, and I'd have time to work out a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching, pay off the car, and buy the seafront flat in about three years. I'd do the joinery qualification in my own time over a couple of years, no rush. I'd use the AI tools for paperwork once they were standard in the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly calm. It's a long way off, and I've got a job I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you uneasier in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hale, the other D&T teacher, retiring and the school not replacing him. If I'm alone, any cut lands on me. Ten years of slow shrinking in the design and technology department worries me more than one big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to start a family in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope so. I'm not seeing anyone right now, but my mum keeps asking. I'd want to be settled with a home and steady work first, the way my parents did it.

say: Ten years is long; today's **pupils will be grown** by then.
Schools should start teaching **practical skills** again.
think: By 2036 I'd have **ten years** in the job, with the workshop safe until 2039.
At **40** I'd still have time for a second trade.
do: Buy the **seafront flat** in about three years after clearing the car loan.
Take the **joinery qualification** slowly over a couple of years.
Use AI for **paperwork** once it's standard at school.
feel: He's **mostly calm**, with some unease at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: Ten years of slow shrinking in the design and technology department worries me more than one big change.
fieldNote: The ten-year picture barely shifts his **home and career plans**.
His deeper worry is **slow attrition** if Mr Hale isn't replaced.
He wants to be **settled first** before a family, like his parents.

steps.text: Buy the seafront flat in about three years
Complete a joinery qualification over two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a trade only buys three years and I'd barely have one by then. What would help is the government paying for proper apprenticeships for adults, not just teenagers. And keeping workshops in schools, so kids still learn to make things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. Making something with your hands gives you a pride a screen never will. If that goes, I don't know what replaces it for lads like the ones I teach.

headlineQuote: Making something with your hands gives you a pride a screen never will.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old D&T teacher** at Northgate Academy in a former shipbuilding town.
He uses AI **now and then** for paperwork and adopts tools once peers prove them.
His long-running worry is **D&T shrinking** for budget reasons, leaving him nearly alone.
In AGI scenarios he leans on **joinery with his dad** as a fallback, though robots reach that too.
He blames **education policy**, and backs apprenticeships over benefits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a trade buys only three years and he'd barely have one.
